strengths: The correlation/probing analysis (SS features vs. EMG power D(E)) is a clean, interpretable experiment, and the layer-wise analysis linking peak correlation to HuBERT layer 6's known effectiveness for discrete resynthesis is an interesting observation.
The k-medoids clustering result showing that EMG power vectors separate by orofacial gesture is a reasonable piece of supporting evidence for the articulatory-encoding hypothesis.

The paper documents a new, larger-vocabulary (6,800 words), natural-speaking-rate (115 wpm) EMG speech corpus that, if released, would be a valuable resource compared to existing small-vocabulary EMG/BCI corpora.
The described data collection protocol (electrode placement, preprocessing, alignment-free CTC training) is described with enough technical detail to be largely followable.
The motivation (non-invasive alternative to invasive BCI speech neuroprostheses) is clinically relevant and well situated relative to prior work.
weaknesses: Despite the title and framing as an end-to-end 'EMG-to-speech synthesis' system, no actual speech-level evaluation is provided: no WER/CER of synthesized speech, no perceptual quality (MOS) metrics, and no synthesized audio samples or spectrograms are shown. The 'Continuing work' section explicitly states these are still being developed, indicating the central claimed contribution is not yet substantiated.

The reported unit error rates (58-64%) and phoneme error rates (41-53%) are very high, raising serious doubt about whether the downstream Tacotron-vocoded audio would be intelligible; the paper provides no evidence (qualitative or quantitative) that the final synthesized speech is usable.

The claim that 'SS models implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms' is overstated relative to the evidence: a linear probe correlation of r=0.85 between SS features and EMG channel power, and separability of gesture clusters, does not rule out confounds such as overall signal intensity/loudness or coarse voicing activity driving the correlation, rather than fine-grained articulatory structure.

It is unclear from the text how many subjects/sessions comprise the main 9-hour, 6,800-word dataset used for the core linear-mapping and synthesis experiments (Sections 5.2-5.3); the 12-participant gesture study in 5.1 appears to be a separate, smaller dataset, and this ambiguity makes it hard to assess generalizability across speakers.

No direct quantitative comparison against prior EMG-to-speech systems (e.g., Gaddy & Klein, Diener et al., Toth et al.) is provided, despite explicit claims of superiority (larger vocabulary, natural speaking rate, alignment-free); the paper only compares its own feature-representation ablations (vec(E), D(E), vec(B)).
Data and code are not yet released ('will be made publicly available upon completion of the project'), limiting reproducibility at the time of review.

The paper reads as a preliminary/interim report (explicit unfinished work, missing key evaluation metrics) rather than a complete study, which limits confidence in the central synthesis claim advertised in the title and abstract.

strengths: The paper reports an interesting empirical finding: EMG power vectors (D(E)) can be linearly mapped from self-supervised speech representations with moderate-to-strong correlation, and this is cross-validated across several SS model families (HuBERT, wav2vec2.0, WavLM) and layer depths, offering an interpretable articulatory lens on SS representations that connects to prior EMA-based probing work.

The creation of a large-vocabulary (~6,800 words), naturalistic-rate (~115 wpm) EMG speech corpus is a potentially valuable contribution to a field that has historically relied on small-vocabulary or private datasets; if released as promised, it could benefit the community.

The paper explicitly identifies real limitations of prior EMG/BCI-to-speech work (small vocabularies, repeated test sentence exposure, unnaturally slow speaking rates, opaque architectures) and frames its data-collection effort as directly addressing these gaps.

The covariance/geodesic-distance formalization of EMG signals and the comparison against alternative EMG features (spectrogram bands) is a reasonably careful and systematic ablation showing D(E)/vec(E) outperform spectrogram-based features for downstream unit/phoneme prediction.
weaknesses: The central claim of the paper -- that the system can 'synthesize speech' from EMG -- is never actually validated. There is no reported audio-based evaluation (no WER/CER, no listening test/MOS, no spectrogram or audio sample comparison); the paper only reports unit error rate (UER) on discrete HuBERT-unit prediction (58-65%) and phoneme error rate (PER, 41-54%), both of which are quite high and are explicitly flagged by the authors themselves in the 'Continuing work' section as still needing perceptual quality assessment. This is a fundamental soundness gap: the paper's title, abstract, and framing promise an EMG-to-speech synthesis system, but no evidence is given that the synthesized audio is intelligible or even recognizable speech.

The main continuous-speech corpus (7,000/1,000/1,660 sentence split) appears to come from a single subject ('the subject articulating...'), which severely limits the generalizability of the emg2speech synthesis results; the 12-subject data used in Section 5.1 is a separate, smaller isolated-gesture dataset, so the flagship synthesis pipeline's single-subject basis is not clearly acknowledged or discussed as a limitation.

Several mechanistic/causal claims are overstated relative to the correlational evidence provided, e.g., the claim that the paper 'provides a principled interpretation' and 'direct explanation' for why HuBERT layer 6 is optimal for resynthesis/language modeling is speculative post-hoc reasoning drawn from a correlation analysis on gesture data, not a causal or ablation-based demonstration.

The reported linear-mapping correlations and clustering accuracies lack statistical context (e.g., no confidence intervals, no per-subject variance reported for k-medoids accuracy of 70.6%/73.7%, no comparison against reasonable non-trivial baselines beyond random chance) that would substantiate 'strong' claims of alignment.

The actual EMG-to-speech synthesis architecture (TDS encoder + CTC + discrete HuBERT units + pretrained Tacotron vocoder) is essentially adopted wholesale from prior BCI-to-speech pipelines ([6],[2],[9]); the technical novelty is limited to the choice of EMG feature representation, and no comparison against a reimplementation of an existing strong baseline (e.g., Gaddy & Klein) is provided for context.

Reproducibility is currently unverifiable: code and data are promised 'upon completion of the project' rather than being available at submission time, and several architectural/training details (hyperparameters, TDS configuration specifics, training procedure for the linear probes) are not fully specified.

The paper is explicitly incomplete by its own admission (Section 6, 'Continuing work' lists core planned experiments -- perceptual quality assessment, WER/CER computation -- as future work), suggesting the submission may be premature for a venue requiring a complete and evidenced contribution.

strengths: Presents a genuinely interesting and quantified scientific finding — a strong linear relationship (r=0.85) between self-supervised speech (S3) model representations and EMG power — that extends prior EMA/articulatory-probing work (Cho et al. 2023/2024) into the EMG modality, and uses it to motivate a concrete architectural choice (EMG covariance/power features as intermediate targets).

Tackles a harder, more clinically realistic problem setting than most prior EMG-to-speech work by not assuming known temporal alignment between EMG and audio, which is important for populations (ALS, laryngectomy) where synchronized audio may be unavailable or unreliable.

Releases what appears to be one of the largest public EMG-to-speech datasets (9h/6800 words healthy participant; ALS participant data; 12-subject orofacial gesture dataset), which is a valuable resource for the field regardless of the modeling results.

Reasonably thorough empirical analysis: layer-wise probing across multiple S3 models, ablations on training-set size, loss curves, phoneme-guided decoding with a statistically significant improvement, and human evaluation (WER/PER/MOS) with multiple independent raters.

Detailed reproducibility appendices covering electrode placement, preprocessing, architecture specification, and optimization hyperparameters, which substantially aids reproducibility despite the data being from clinical/single-subject settings.
Honest and detailed limitations and appendix discussion contextualizing WER against related BCI/EMG literature without overclaiming direct comparability.
weaknesses: The audio 'ground truth' targets are synthesized via gTTS from text transcripts rather than the participant's own recorded speech (even for the healthy participant who audibly vocalized), meaning the system is trained to reproduce a generic TTS voice's phoneme/unit sequence rather than genuinely idiosyncratic prosody/expressive content the paper claims audio A encodes; this weakens the claimed 'direct EMG-to-audio' framing and makes some of the linear-mapping/S3 analyses (done on real vocalized audio) inconsistent with the synthesis pipeline (done on gTTS audio), which is a design tension not fully resolved.

Reported intelligibility is low (mean human-transcribed WER ~61-63% for the healthy/general corpus and ~51% for ALS), and the paper's own comparisons show these rates are not clearly better than, and are sometimes worse than, prior EMG or even invasive BCI systems, making the practical advance of the proposed method unclear beyond the analysis contribution.

Core results rely on a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant (plus a separate 12-subject gesture dataset used only for the clustering/covariance analysis, not for the end-to-end synthesis results), which sharply limits generalizability of the synthesis performance claims and the clinical relevance narrative.

The claim that 'S3 models implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms as reflected in EMG activity' rests on a linear correlation between S3 features and EMG power (D(E)), which could partly reflect shared coarse energy/loudness/voicing-activity co-variation rather than fine-grained articulatory structure specifically; no control analysis (e.g., regressing out simple audio energy/pitch envelope) is provided to rule out this simpler explanation.

Cross-study WER/PER comparisons to prior BCI and EMG systems (Section 2.1, Appendix C) are explicitly acknowledged by the authors as not directly comparable due to differing corpora, alignment assumptions, and evaluation protocols, yet these comparisons are used repeatedly to contextualize and implicitly support the paper's contribution, which risks conflating narrative framing with rigorous benchmarking.

MOS evaluation is conducted on only a small subset of test sentences (35 of 460) with 10 raters and no reported inter-rater reliability statistics, and the paper's own explanation (that MOS mainly reflects vocoder naturalness rather than linguistic fidelity) suggests MOS is not a strong indicator of the method's core claims.

The work's core methodological content (EMG signal processing, articulatory-mechanism analysis, phoneme/CTC decoding of a physiological signal) is arguably more aligned with speech/BCI/signal-processing venues than a computational linguistics conference, and beyond using pretrained S3 models and phoneme lookup tables, the NLP-specific methodological contribution is limited.

strengths: Introduces one of the largest publicly available EMG-to-speech datasets (~9 hours, >6800 words from a healthy participant, plus ~1 hour/300 words from an ALS participant), along with a 12-subject orofacial gesture dataset, code, and demos — a substantial and useful community resource.

The core empirical finding — that self-supervised speech (S3) representations linearly predict EMG power (r=0.85) and that EMG power vectors cluster by articulatory gesture — is a novel and interesting result that helps explain prior observations (e.g., why HuBERT layer 6 is favored for discrete resynthesis) and motivates the proposed pipeline in a principled way.

Tackles the more clinically realistic and technically harder alignment-free EMG-to-audio problem (no assumed frame-level EMG-audio correspondence), unlike most prior EMG-to-speech work, and validates this on a genuine ALS patient producing silent speech.

Reasonably thorough ablations and evaluation: unit/phoneme error rates, phoneme-guided decoding with statistically significant improvement, multiple human transcribers for WER, MOS ratings, training-size scaling analysis, and an EMG2TEXT/WFST comparison — supporting reproducibility and interpretability of the results.

Honest and detailed discussion of why direct comparisons to prior EMG/BCI speech interfaces are not apples-to-apples, and a well-written limitations/ethics section acknowledging single-subject clinical evaluation, lack of longitudinal robustness testing, and absence of large-scale pretraining.
weaknesses: All primary decoding/synthesis results rest on a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant (n=1 each); the only multi-subject analysis (gesture clustering, n=12) is a separate, simpler task, limiting claims about generalizability of the EMG-to-speech system itself.

Training targets (dis(H)_HuBERT units) are derived from gTTS text-to-speech audio rather than the participant's own recorded speech, so the 'speech' being synthesized largely reflects generic vocoder output driven by decoded phonemic content rather than the participant's actual vocal characteristics; this blurs the distinction between the proposed system and a simpler EMG-to-text-then-TTS pipeline (which the authors' own EMG2TEXT ablation partially confirms is competitive or better).

No same-data, matched-condition baseline (e.g., re-implementing Gaddy & Klein or a standard spectrogram-based EMG-to-speech model on this exact dataset) is provided to isolate the benefit of the proposed articulatory/covariance-based representation versus alternative architectures; cross-paper WER comparisons are explicitly flagged as non-comparable, leaving the central efficacy claim only loosely supported.

Reported WERs remain high (51-62%), and the disconnect between high WER and relatively high MOS (3.79) — attributed to the vocoder always producing plausible-sounding speech regardless of decoding accuracy — raises questions about how informative MOS is as a quality metric in this setting.

The claim that S3 models 'implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms' rests on correlational linear-probing evidence; while suggestive and consistent with related EMA literature, alternative explanations (e.g., shared dependence on phonetic/prosodic content rather than a direct articulatory encoding) are not ruled out.
